Brazil’s National Data Protection Authority (ANPD) has ordered Discord to suspend its "Go Live" feature and all equivalent video streaming tools across the country within three business days.

The platform itself is not blocked. Text chat, voice channels and other core functions remain fully available to Brazilian users. The suspension will stay in place until Discord proves it has implemented effective safeguards to protect children and adolescents.

The decision follows an investigation into child safety failures linked to the death of a 13-year-old girl in Naviraí (Mato Grosso do Sul) on 22 July. Authorities say she was encouraged to take her own life during a roughly 45-minute private Discord livestream. Five teenagers and one 18-year-old have been arrested in connection with the case (Operation Lívia). ANPD cited Discord’s lack of real-time access to livestream content, which prevents automated detection of violations, as well as reliance on flawed systems and user reports.

First Lady Janja da Silva had publicly called for a full ban of the platform days earlier. Discord described the order as "premature," stating it is carefully reviewing the measure, continues to cooperate with law enforcement, and confirmed it quickly removed the private server involved. The company noted that some of the activity was coordinated on other platforms.

Failure to comply could result in fines of up to 50 million reais (approximately $9.7 million) per violation. Discord has 10 business days to appeal. A complete ban of the platform would still require a court decision.

My son announced on Tuesday evening, during dinner, that for Halloween he wanted to dress up as a fart.

I literally almost choked on the water I was drinking. He’s six years old. He was just sitting there, serious, with spaghetti sauce on his chin, saying: “I want to be a big brown fart cloud.” My husband looked at me like it was my job to handle the situation. I didn’t know what to say. Where do kids even get these ideas? I told him absolutely not. To pick something normal — a superhero, a dinosaur, anything else. He made that stubborn face that means “he’s never going to let this go.”

He started explaining to me, with the utmost seriousness, that farts are funny, that everyone would laugh, and that it would be the best costume ever. I was exhausted after work, my head was pounding, and I lost my patience. I said: fine. You want to be a fart? Make it yourself. I’ll help you find the materials, but the rest is up to you. I thought he’d give up after ten minutes. He didn’t.
He spent the next three days in the living room, working with brown and beige fabrics I helped him order, because apparently he needed “fart-colored tulle” — a phrase I never thought I’d say. He watched tutorials on my phone about how to gather fabric, asked me for help with the knots, but insisted on arranging every single layer himself. He got frustrated twice, was close to crying, but kept going. His little hands working carefully, his tongue between his teeth as he focused.

Yesterday he finished. He put it on and strutted around the house, proudly showing it off to his father and grandmother, who both looked absolutely stunned. I thought I’d be embarrassed, but instead I felt a strange pride. My son said he wanted to be a fart, I told him to figure it out himself, and he… actually did it.

He’s been sleeping in it for two nights. Two neighbors have already asked if I can make one for their kids, too. I told them he’s taking orders now. Eight dollars per cloud. He’s never been so confident in his life.

Walmart is selling real diamond earrings for $12.

Not a typo. Half-carat lab-grown diamonds, same carbon, graded by the same labs that grade the stone in your engagement ring. A jeweler can't tell them apart without a machine.

And that $12 price tag is why the company that invented the engagement ring is about to get sold for scrap.

De Beers ran the diamond trade for over a century. At its peak it controlled up to 90% of the world's rough supply, and when demand dipped it just locked diamonds in London vaults until prices came back. The slogan "A Diamond Is Forever" came from their ad agency in 1947. So did the rule that a ring should cost two months of your salary. Before that campaign, most American brides never got a diamond at all.

The whole thing held for 80 years because there were only so many mines. Then China started growing diamonds in reactors, and there's no vault on earth big enough to hide a factory's output.

Lab-grown wholesale prices have crashed roughly 96% from their peak, down to around $100 a carat. The Knot says 61% of engagement rings sold in 2025 had lab-grown center stones, up 239% since 2020. Even De Beers' own average selling price fell 32% in a year, to $105 a carat.

So Anglo American, which owns De Beers, has written it down by $6.8 billion in two years and is now in talks to sell the whole thing for about $1 billion. This is a company that was valued over $18 billion in 2001 and $13 billion as recently as 2011.

The stones coming out of the ground are the same as ever. The only scarce thing De Beers ever owned was the marketing, and marketing doesn't survive a $12 price tag at Walmart.

I watched the F1 film with Brad Pitt the other day, and there’s a moment where his character asks to add something to the car that isn’t really in the rules. The FIA punishes it, but the team can still race with the earlier car. It made me think.

In F1, the best teams live at the edge of the regulations. Sometimes the FIA allows what they’ve found, and sometimes it says that goes too far. Occasionally the rules are rewritten afterwards.

Now, City. I’m not defending them. A commission found they entered into sham agreements and broke the spending limits. A sham is an arrangement that isn’t what it claims to be, so that’s a different thing from using a gap nobody had spotted.

City deny it and will appeal. But I find it useful to ask/reflect on how people inside the club see it.

From their point of view, PERHAPS they believe they were doing what elite competitors do: looking at the rules, finding the limits, challenging interpretations and moving faster than the regulatory system.

From the outside, you might look at that and say, “That’s cheating.” From inside the organisation, they might say, “We found something nobody had thought of.”

If you believe you’ve found a way to bring money in, more or less within the rules (and the commission said it was not in the rules and it was cheating), you might tell yourself you’re just being a sharp competitor.

We are all asking “did City cheat?”. But I find this question interesting too: “how did City come to believe they weren’t?”

And understanding a mindset, or trying to, isn’t excusing it.

‘World’s Largest Time Capsule’ opened after 50 years... 

In 1977, a Boy Scout troop in Seward, Nebraska, created one of the most unusual time capsules of the era. Instead of burying letters or small artifacts, they entombed a brand-new 1977 Chevrolet Vega, along with period items such as soda bottles, newspapers, and a small motorcycle. The project, organized by Troop 256, reflected both the optimism of the late 1970s and the fascination with preserving contemporary culture for future generations.

The car itself, priced at just over $3,000 according to the original dealer sticker, was sealed in a concrete vault, wrapped in protective plastic, and surrounded by memorabilia meant to capture the spirit of the time. The walls were decorated with Scout troop names and painted murals, giving the capsule the feel of both a monument and a playful experiment in historical preservation.

You owe the IRS $100,000

They'll take $5,000 and close your file. Permanently. Balance goes to $0

It's called an Offer in Compromise. Form 656. The IRS approved 42% of them last year. Application fee: $205

Here's the exact formula they use to decide your number and how to reverse-engineer the lowest possible offer

The IRS doesn't want to chase you for 10 years. Liens require court filings. Levies require processing. Garnishments require administration. They'd rather take your $5,000 check today than spend a decade trying to squeeze $100,000 out of someone who will never have it

They literally built a math formula to calculate the minimum they'll accept. Here it is:

RCP = (monthly disposable income x remaining collection months) + (net realizable equity in assets)

Monthly disposable income: your gross monthly income minus IRS-allowed living expenses. They don't use YOUR actual expenses. They use standardized tables published on the IRS website. These tables set exact allowances by county for housing, food, transportation, healthcare, and out-of-pocket expenses

If you earn $4,200/month and the IRS allowable expense table for your county totals $3,900, your disposable income is $300/month. If you earn $3,800/month and the table allows $3,900, your disposable income is negative and the IRS considers it $0

Remaining collection months: for a lump sum offer (paid in 5 months or less), multiply disposable income by 12. For a periodic payment offer (paid over 6-24 months), multiply by 24. A lump sum offer will always be cheaper than a payment plan offer. Always choose lump sum if you can

Net realizable equity in assets: bank accounts, investments, vehicles, real property. BUT they subtract allowances. Household furnishings: exempt. Retirement accounts: heavily discounted, because the IRS applies a "quick sale value" and knows cashing them out triggers penalties and taxes

Real calculation:

Income: $4,200/month
IRS allowed expenses: $3,900/month
Disposable income: $300/month

Lump sum multiplier: 12 months
$300 x 12 = $3,600

Assets:
Bank account: $2,100
Car equity: $4,800 (below the IRS allowance, counts as $0)
Household goods: exempt

RCP: $3,600 + $2,100 = $5,700

Your offer: $5,700 on $100,000 in tax debt. 5.7 cents on the dollar

The nuclear part:

While the offer is being reviewed (6-24 months), collection activity legally stops. No levies. No wage garnishment. This is in IRC Section 6331(k)(1)

And if the IRS fails to make a determination within 24 months of receiving your application, your offer is AUTOMATICALLY ACCEPTED. Two years of silence = you win by default. IRC Section 7122(f)

The forms you need:

Form 433-A (OIC): complete financial disclosure. Every bank account, every asset, every income source, every expense. Fill it out accurately because they cross-reference it against bank and DMV records. Lying on this form is a federal crime

Form 656: the actual offer. Your amount, your payment terms, your signature

$205 application fee (waived if your income is low enough. the form has the table)

Initial payment with the application: 20% of your offer for lump sum. On a $5,700 offer that's $1,140
